slides.narration: Pull a woollen jumper over your head on a dry winter evening and you hear crackles and may see tiny sparks. Those sparks come from electric charge moved from one material to another. In this part we look at what charge is, the law that gives the force between two charges, how several forces combine, and the idea of an electric field filling the space around a charge.

slides.heading: Frictional electricity
slides.body_md: Rubbing two different materials together transfers **electrons** from one to the other:
bullets: The material that **gains** electrons becomes **negative**; the one that **loses** them becomes equally **positive**.
A glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positive; an ebonite rod rubbed with fur becomes negative.
Only electrons move: the positive nuclei stay fixed in the materials.

slides.narration: When two materials rub, electrons near the surface of one are held more loosely than in the other, and some cross over. Glass rubbed with silk loses electrons and becomes positive, while the silk becomes negative by exactly the same amount. Ebonite rubbed with fur gains electrons. Nothing is created: charge is only moved, and it is always the light electrons that move, never the nuclei.

slides.heading: Conductors, insulators and two kinds of charge
slides.body_md: Charges are of **two kinds**, positive and negative: like charges **repel**, unlike charges **attract**.
bullets: **Conductors** (metals, the human body, salt water) have charges free to move through them.
**Insulators** (glass, plastic, dry air) hold their charges in place where they are put.
A charged rod picks up bits of paper because it pulls their charges slightly apart (polarises them) and then attracts the nearer, opposite side.

slides.narration: There are only two kinds of charge. Two positive or two negative charges push apart; a positive and a negative pull together. In a metal, electrons wander freely, so charge spreads over it at once: a conductor. In plastic or glass, charge stays where it is rubbed on: an insulator. A charged comb attracts scraps of paper by separating their charges a little and pulling on the nearer, opposite side.

slides.heading: Quantisation and conservation of charge
slides.body_md:
**Quantisation:** every charge is a whole-number multiple of the electronic charge,
$$q = n e,\qquad e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C},\quad n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$$
**Conservation:** the total charge of an isolated system never changes; charge is only transferred.
bullets: Because e is tiny, everyday charges contain huge numbers of electrons, so charge seems continuous.
In pair production a photon becomes an electron and a positron: total charge stays zero.

rows: q = n e, n an integer
Total charge of an isolated system is constant
Total charge is the algebraic sum
Same in every frame of reference

visual.alt: Table of four properties of charge: quantised, conserved, additive and invariant

slides.narration: Charge comes in lumps. Every charge ever measured is a whole number times one point six times ten to the minus nineteen coulomb, the charge on an electron. A charge of a microcoulomb contains about six million million of these lumps, so in everyday life charge looks smooth. And charge is conserved: rubbing, reactions and even the creation of new particles always leave the total unchanged.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is that charge possible?
slides.body_md: (a) Can a body carry a charge of $2.4 \times 10^{-19}$ C? (b) A plastic rod gains a charge of $-3.2$ nC by rubbing. How many electrons did it gain?
bullets: (a) $n = \dfrac{q}{e} = \dfrac{2.4 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.5$: not a whole number, so **impossible**.
(b) $n = \dfrac{|q|}{e} = \dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-9}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.0 \times 10^{10}$ electrons.

visual.alt: Worked table: 2.4 times ten to the minus nineteen coulomb is one and a half electronic charges, impossible; minus 3.2 nanocoulombs is twenty billion electrons

slides.narration: Divide the charge by the electronic charge. Two point four times ten to the minus nineteen gives one and a half, and no object can carry half an electron’s charge, so that value is impossible. The rod’s charge of minus three point two nanocoulombs means it gained twenty billion extra electrons, a huge number, yet its mass changed by an amount far too small to weigh.

slides.heading: Coulomb’s law
slides.body_md:
The force between two point charges is along the line joining them, proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation:
$$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2},\qquad \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2}$$
bullets: $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ C² N⁻¹ m⁻² is the **permittivity of free space**.
One **coulomb** is the charge that exerts $9 \times 10^{9}$ N on an equal charge 1 m away in vacuum.
Vector form: $\vec F_{12} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\hat r_{12}$, where $\hat r_{12}$ points from $q_1$ to $q_2$ (force on $q_2$).

slides.narration: Coulomb measured the force between small charged spheres with a delicate torsion balance. The force grows with each charge and falls off as the square of the distance, just like gravity. The constant one over four pi epsilon nought is nine times ten to the nine in SI units, so two charges of one coulomb a metre apart would push with nine billion newtons. Real charges are far smaller.

slides.heading: In a medium, and compared with gravity
slides.body_md: In a medium of relative permittivity (dielectric constant) $K = \varepsilon/\varepsilon_0$, the force is reduced: $F_m = \dfrac{F_\text{vacuum}}{K}$.
columns:
**Coulomb force**
- Acts between charges
- Attractive or repulsive
- Depends on the medium
- Very strong

**Gravitational force**
- Acts between masses
- Always attractive
- Independent of the medium
- Very weak

visual.alt: Table of approximate dielectric constants: vacuum 1, air just above 1, transformer oil 2.5, glass 5 to 10, water 80

slides.narration: Put the charges in oil or water and the force drops by the dielectric constant K, because the medium’s molecules line up and partly cancel the field. In water, with K about eighty, salts dissolve because the attraction between their ions is cut eighty times. Both Coulomb’s law and Newton’s law of gravitation are inverse-square laws, but the electric force can repel as well as attract and is enormously stronger.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: in air and in oil
slides.body_md: Charges of $+2.0\ \mu$C and $-5.0\ \mu$C are 15 cm apart. Find the force between them in vacuum and in transformer oil ($K = 2.5$).
bullets: Step 1 — $F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.15)^2} = 4.0$ N, attractive.
Step 2 — $F_m = \dfrac{F}{K} = \dfrac{4.0}{2.5} = 1.6$ N, still attractive.

slides.narration: Since both forces fall off as the square of the distance, their ratio does not depend on how far apart the protons are. Putting in the numbers, the electric push is about a million million million million million million times the gravitational pull. slides.heading: The electric field
slides.body_md:
The **electric field** at a point is the force per unit positive test charge placed there:
$$\vec E = \lim_{q_0 \to 0}\dfrac{\vec F}{q_0},\qquad \text{unit N C}^{-1}\ (= \text{V m}^{-1})$$
Point charge: $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}$, radially outward for $q > 0$. A charge $q$ in a field feels $\vec F = q\vec E$.
bullets: The test charge is kept tiny so that it does not disturb the charges producing the field.
Fields of several charges add as vectors (superposition).

visual.alt: Field strength of a point charge against distance: it falls as one over r squared, to a quarter when the distance doubles
visual.caption: Doubling r divides E by 4; tripling r divides it by 9.

slides.narration: Instead of thinking of one charge reaching across space to push another, we say every charge sets up an electric field around it. The field at a point is the force a tiny positive test charge would feel there, per coulomb. For a point charge it falls off as one over r squared. Any charge placed in the field then feels a force q times E.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: where is the field zero?
slides.body_md: Charges of $+8$ nC and $+2$ nC are 0.30 m apart. Find (a) the point between them where the field is zero, (b) the field at the midpoint.
bullets: (a) At distance $x$ from the 8 nC charge: $\dfrac{8}{x^2} = \dfrac{2}{(0.30 - x)^2}$, so $\dfrac{0.30 - x}{x} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x = 0.20$ m.
(b) $E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9}(8 - 2) \times 10^{-9}}{(0.15)^2} = 2400$ N C$^{-1}$, pointing away from the 8 nC charge.

visual.alt: Field lines of two equal positive charges with a neutral point between them

slides.narration: Between two positive charges their fields point in opposite directions, so somewhere they cancel. Setting the two field sizes equal and taking square roots, the neutral point is twice as far from the big charge as from the small one: twenty centimetres from the eight nanocoulomb charge. At the midpoint the bigger charge wins, leaving a net field of two thousand four hundred newtons per coulomb.

slides.heading: Charge densities
slides.body_md: For charge spread continuously over a body, we describe how densely it is spread:
bullets: A wire 2.0 m long carrying 6.0 μC has λ = 3.0 μC m⁻¹ (if uniform).
The field of such a distribution is found by adding (integrating) the fields of tiny elements dq.

visual.alt: Table of linear, surface and volume charge densities with their definitions and SI units

slides.narration: A charged wire, plate or ball is made of so many charges that we treat the charge as spread smoothly. Along a wire we use the linear density lambda, charge per metre. Over a surface we use sigma, charge per square metre. Through a volume we use rho, charge per cubic metre. In the next chapter, Gauss’s theorem lets us find the fields of such distributions easily.

slides.body_md: Key results:

Net force = vector sum of pair forces
λ (C m⁻¹), σ (C m⁻²), ρ (C m⁻³)

slides.narration: To sum up: rubbing moves electrons, and charge is quantised and conserved. Coulomb’s law gives an inverse-square force, reduced by the dielectric constant in a medium and vastly stronger than gravity. Forces from several charges add as vectors. bullets: Convert μC and nC to coulombs and cm to metres before substituting.
In superposition problems draw a diagram with each force arrow, then add components.
State directions: attraction or repulsion, and “away from” or “towards” for fields.
For a null point between like charges, take square roots of the charges’ ratio.

rows: No: not a multiple of e

slides.heading: Field lines and dipoles
slides.body_md: Part 2 — drawing fields with lines, and the simplest charge arrangement that appears everywhere in chemistry and physics: the dipole.

visual.alt: Field lines of an electric dipole
visual.caption: Traced numerically; arrowheads checked against the computed field.

slides.narration: Faraday pictured the space round charges as filled with lines of force, and the picture is still the best way to see a field. In this part we learn the rules those lines obey and the patterns they make. Then we study the electric dipole, a pair of equal and opposite charges, find its field along two special directions, and see how it behaves in a uniform field.

slides.heading: Properties of electric lines of force
slides.body_md: An electric line of force is a curve whose **tangent** at every point gives the direction of $\vec E$ there.
bullets: Lines start on **positive** charges and end on **negative** charges (or at infinity).
**Two lines never intersect**: at a crossing the field would have two directions at once.
Lines are **closer together** where the field is **stronger**.
Electrostatic field lines **never form closed loops**, and they meet a conductor’s surface at right angles.

visual.alt: Radial field lines of a positive point charge
visual.caption: Traced numerically from Coulomb’s law.

slides.narration: A line of force is drawn so that at every point its direction shows the way the field points. The rules are simple. Lines leave positive charges and arrive at negative ones. They never cross, because a field can point only one way at a point. Where lines crowd together the field is strong, and where they spread out it is weak. And electrostatic field lines never close on themselves.

slides.heading: Patterns: point charges and parallel plates
slides.body_md: Standard patterns:
bullets: Isolated positive charge: radial lines outward; negative charge: radial lines inward.
Two oppositely charged parallel plates: **straight, parallel, equally spaced** lines between them — a **uniform field** — with some bending (fringing) at the edges.

visual.alt: Radial field lines ending on a negative point charge

slides.narration: Round a single positive charge the lines spread straight outwards like spokes, and round a negative charge they point straight in. Between two large parallel plates with opposite charges, the lines run straight across from the positive plate to the negative one, evenly spaced: the field there is the same everywhere, a uniform field. Only near the edges do the lines bulge outwards.

slides.heading: Patterns: a dipole and two like charges
slides.body_md: Two equal and opposite charges: lines curve from + to −. Two equal like charges: lines bend away from each other, leaving a **neutral point** midway where $E = 0$.

visual.alt: Field lines of two equal positive charges with a neutral point between them

slides.narration: For a positive and a negative charge, lines leave the positive one and curve round to end on the negative one, crowded together between them. For two equal positive charges the lines from each are pushed away from the other, and right in the middle there is a point with no field at all, called the neutral point. A small test charge placed there would feel no force.

slides.heading: The electric dipole
slides.body_md:
Two equal and opposite charges $+q$ and $-q$ a small distance $2a$ apart form an **electric dipole**. Its **dipole moment** is
$$\vec p = q \times 2a\,\hat p,\qquad \text{directed from } -q \text{ to } +q,\ \text{unit C m}$$
bullets: Net charge zero, yet it produces a field because the two charges are at different places.
Many molecules (H₂O, HCl) are permanent dipoles; others become dipoles in a field.

visual.alt: Field lines of an electric dipole
visual.caption: Traced numerically; arrowheads checked against the computed field.

slides.narration: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges a small distance apart. Its strength is measured by the dipole moment, the charge times the separation, pointing from the negative charge to the positive one. A water molecule is a natural dipole, because its oxygen end is slightly negative and its hydrogen end slightly positive. The total charge is zero, but the field is not.

slides.heading: Field on the axial line
slides.body_md:
At P on the axis, distance $r$ from the centre: $E_+ = \dfrac{kq}{(r - a)^2}$ along $\vec p$, $E_- = \dfrac{kq}{(r + a)^2}$ opposite. So
$$E_\text{axial} = kq\left[\dfrac{1}{(r - a)^2} - \dfrac{1}{(r + a)^2}\right] = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2pr}{(r^2 - a^2)^2}$$
For $r \gg a$: $E_\text{axial} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{r^3}$, along $\vec p$.

slides.narration: At a point on the axis beyond the positive charge, the positive charge is nearer, so its outward field beats the inward field of the negative charge. Subtracting the two and simplifying gives two p r over the square of r squared minus a squared. Far away, a squared is negligible beside r squared and the field becomes two k p over r cubed, pointing along the dipole moment.

slides.heading: Field on the equatorial line
slides.body_md:
At Q on the perpendicular bisector, distance $r$: both fields have size $\dfrac{kq}{r^2 + a^2}$; their components along the bisector cancel and those parallel to the axis add:
$$E_\text{eq} = 2\dfrac{kq}{r^2 + a^2}\cdot\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{r^2 + a^2}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{(r^2 + a^2)^{3/2}}$$
For $r \gg a$: $E_\text{eq} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^3}$, **opposite** to $\vec p$.

slides.narration: On the line perpendicular to the dipole through its centre, both charges are the same distance away, so their fields are equal in size. Their sideways parts cancel and their parts parallel to the axis add, pointing from plus towards minus. The result is p over the cube of root r squared plus a squared, which becomes k p over r cubed far away, opposite to p and half the axial value.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: fields of a small dipole
slides.body_md: Charges of $\pm 5.0$ nC are 4.0 mm apart. Find the field 0.20 m from the centre (a) on the axis, (b) on the equatorial line.
bullets: Step 1 — $p = 5.0 \times 10^{-9} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} = 2.0 \times 10^{-11}$ C m; since $0.20 \gg 0.002$, use the short-dipole forms.
(a) $E_\text{ax} = \dfrac{2kp}{r^3} = \dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^{9} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-11}}{(0.20)^3} = 45$ N C$^{-1}$, along $\vec p$.
(b) $E_\text{eq} = \dfrac{kp}{r^3} = 22.5$ N C$^{-1}$, opposite to $\vec p$.

The point is a hundred times farther than the half-separation, so the short-dipole formulas are fine. On the axis, two k p over r cubed gives forty five newtons per coulomb along p. On the equatorial line the field is exactly half, twenty two and a half, pointing the opposite way.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: when is a dipole “short”?
slides.body_md: For charges $\pm 2.0$ nC 2.0 cm apart ($a = 1.0$ cm), compare the exact axial field at $r = 3.0$ cm with the short-dipole formula.
bullets: Step 2 — exact: $\dfrac{2kpr}{(r^2 - a^2)^2} = \dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^{9} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-11} \times 0.030}{(0.0009 - 0.0001)^2} \approx 3.38 \times 10^{4}$ N C$^{-1}$.
Step 3 — short-dipole: $\dfrac{2kp}{r^3} \approx 2.67 \times 10^{4}$ N C$^{-1}$; the exact value is 1.27 times larger, so the approximation fails at $r = 3a$.

visual.alt: Ratio of the exact axial field of a dipole to the short-dipole formula against distance: well above 1 close to the dipole, and within a few per cent of 1 once r is several times a
visual.caption: The short-dipole result 2kp/r³ is reliable only when r ≫ a.

slides.narration: At only three times the half-separation, the exact axial field comes out about twenty seven per cent bigger than the short-dipole formula. The graph shows how the ratio approaches one as you move away: by about ten times a, the error is down to a couple of per cent. Use the simple formula only when the point is far from the dipole compared with its length.

slides.heading: Dipole in a uniform field
slides.body_md:
In a uniform field $\vec E$, the forces $+q\vec E$ and $-q\vec E$ are equal and opposite: **net force zero**, but they form a **couple**:
$$\tau = qE \times 2a\sin\theta = pE\sin\theta,\qquad \vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E$$
bullets: The torque turns $\vec p$ towards $\vec E$; it is maximum ($pE$) at θ = 90° and zero at 0° and 180°.
In a **non-uniform** field there is also a net force, so the dipole moves as well as turns.

The positive end is pushed along the field and the negative end the other way with an equal force, so the dipole as a whole does not move off. slides.body_md: Key results:

slides.narration: To sum up: field lines run from positive to negative charges, never cross and crowd together where the field is strong. A dipole’s moment points from minus to plus. sections.heading: 1. Electric charge
sections.body_md:
- **Frictional electricity:** rubbing transfers **electrons**; the gainer becomes negative, the loser equally positive (glass–silk: glass +; ebonite–fur: ebonite −).
- Two kinds of charge: like charges repel, unlike attract. **Conductors** let charge move freely; **insulators** do not.
- **Quantisation:** $q = n e$, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C, n an integer. **Conservation:** the total charge of an isolated system is constant. Charge is also additive and the same in all frames.

key_terms.definition_md: Every charge is an integral multiple of the electronic charge e.
The net charge of an isolated system remains constant.

sections.heading: 2. Coulomb’s law and superposition
sections.body_md:
- $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$, $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^{9}$ N m² C⁻², $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; along the line joining the charges.
- Vector form: $\vec F_{12} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\hat r_{12}$ (force on $q_2$, $\hat r_{12}$ from $q_1$ to $q_2$); $\vec F_{21} = -\vec F_{12}$.
- In a medium: $F_m = F/K$, with $K = \varepsilon/\varepsilon_0$ (dielectric constant, relative permittivity).
- **Coulomb**: the charge that exerts $9 \times 10^{9}$ N on an equal charge 1 m away in vacuum.
- Compared with gravitation: both inverse-square and central; electric force can attract or repel, depends on the medium, and is about $10^{36}$ times stronger between two protons.
- **Superposition:** the net force on a charge is the vector sum of the forces due to each other charge, each found as if the others were absent.

sections.heading: 3. Electric field and charge densities
sections.body_md:
- $\vec E = \lim_{q_0 \to 0}\vec F/q_0$; unit N C⁻¹ = V m⁻¹. A charge in a field feels $\vec F = q\vec E$.
- Point charge: $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}$, radially outward for $q > 0$, inward for $q < 0$. Several charges: vector sum.
- Between two like charges $q_1$, $q_2$ distance $d$ apart, $E = 0$ at $x = \dfrac{d\sqrt{q_1}}{\sqrt{q_1} + \sqrt{q_2}}$ from $q_1$.
- Charge densities: linear $\lambda = dq/dl$ (C m⁻¹), surface $\sigma = dq/dA$ (C m⁻²), volume $\rho = dq/dV$ (C m⁻³).

sections.heading: 4. Electric lines of force
sections.body_md:
- Tangent gives the direction of $\vec E$; lines start on + charges and end on − charges (or at infinity).
- Two lines **never intersect** (unique direction of $\vec E$ at a point); they are **denser** where E is larger; electrostatic lines **never form closed loops**; they meet a conductor normally.
- Patterns: radial for a point charge; curved from + to − for a dipole; bending apart with a **neutral point** for two like charges; straight, parallel and equally spaced (uniform field) between oppositely charged parallel plates.

key_terms.definition_md: A point where the resultant electric field is zero.

sections.heading: 5. Electric dipole
sections.body_md:
- Dipole: $+q$ and $-q$ separated by $2a$; moment $\vec p = q(2a)$ from $-q$ to $+q$ (C m).
- **Axial point** (distance r from centre): $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2pr}{(r^2 - a^2)^2} \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{r^3}$, along $\vec p$.
- **Equatorial point:** $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{(r^2 + a^2)^{3/2}} \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^3}$, opposite to $\vec p$. For a short dipole, $E_\text{axial} = 2E_\text{eq}$ at the same r.
- **Uniform field:** net force zero; torque $\vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E$, $\tau = pE\sin\theta$ (max $pE$ at 90°, zero at 0° and 180°); the dipole rotates to align with E but does not translate. In a non-uniform field there is also a net force.

key_terms.definition_md: Product of either charge and the separation, directed from −q to +q.

questions.stem_md: A glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth. The silk becomes negatively charged because

options.text_md: electrons move from the glass to the silk
protons move from the silk to the glass
negative charge is created in the silk by friction
electrons move from the silk to the glass

questions.stem_md: A plastic comb drawn through dry hair acquires a charge of −4.8 × 10⁻⁸ C. How many extra electrons does it carry? Give the answer in units of 10¹¹.
A metal sphere is given a charge of −1.0 μC by adding electrons. By how much does its mass increase? Give the answer in units of 10⁻¹⁸ kg (3 significant figures). (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.)
True or false? When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, positive charge is created on the glass and negative charge on the silk.
questions.solution_md: False. No charge is created: electrons are transferred from glass to silk, and the total charge stays zero (conservation of charge).

questions.stem_md: A positively charged rod is brought near (without touching) one end of an uncharged, insulated metal bar. The near end of the bar becomes

options.text_md: positively charged, and the far end negatively charged
negatively charged, and the far end positively charged
negatively charged, and the far end stays neutral
uncharged, because the rod does not touch it

questions.solution_md: Free electrons in the metal are attracted towards the rod, leaving the far end short of electrons — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A charged plastic ruler picks up small bits of uncharged paper. Explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: The charged ruler **polarises** each bit of paper: charges in the paper shift slightly, so the side **nearer** the ruler carries charge **opposite** to the ruler’s and the far side the same charge. The attraction on the nearer charges is **stronger** (smaller distance) than the repulsion on the farther ones, so there is a **net attraction**.

questions.solution_md: Polarisation; nearer charges attract more strongly.

marking_scheme.step: Paper polarised: opposite charge on the near side

questions.stem_md: Two identical small conducting spheres carry +8.0 μC and −2.0 μC. They are touched together and separated. How many electrons pass to the first sphere? Give the answer in units of 10¹³ (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Total charge $= 8.0 - 2.0 = 6.0\ \mu$C, shared equally: each gets $+3.0\ \mu$C. The first sphere’s charge falls by $5.0\ \mu$C, so $n = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-6}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.13 \times 10^{13}$, i.e. $\dfrac{3.13 \times 10^{13}}{10^{13}} = 3.13$.

marking_scheme.step: Each sphere ends with +3.0 μC (conservation, symmetry)

answer.model_answer_md: $\vec F_{12} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\hat r_{12}$, where $\hat r_{12}$ is the unit vector from $q_1$ to $q_2$. Similarly $\vec F_{21} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\hat r_{21}$. Since $\hat r_{21} = -\hat r_{12}$, $\vec F_{21} = -\vec F_{12}$: equal and opposite.

questions.stem_md: Give one similarity and two differences between Coulomb’s law of electrostatic force and Newton’s law of gravitation.

Field of +q at P: $E_+ = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{(r - a)^2}$, along BP (along p). Field of −q: $E_- = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{(r + a)^2}$, towards A. Net: $E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{1}{(r - a)^2} - \dfrac{1}{(r + a)^2}\right] = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{4qar}{(r^2 - a^2)^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2pr}{(r^2 - a^2)^2}$, along p. questions.stem_md: The electric field at a point on the axis of a short dipole, 10 cm from its centre, is 360 N C⁻¹. Find the dipole moment, in units of 10⁻¹¹ C m.
questions.solution_md: $E = \dfrac{2kp}{r^3} \Rightarrow p = \dfrac{Er^3}{2k} = \dfrac{360 \times (0.10)^3}{2 \times 9 \times 10^{9}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-11}$ C m, i.e. $\dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-11}}{10^{-11}} = 2.0$.

questions.stem_md: A proton and an electron are released from rest in the same uniform electric field. Compared with the proton, the electron has

options.text_md: an acceleration about 1840 times larger, in the opposite direction
the same acceleration in the opposite direction
the same acceleration in the same direction

questions.solution_md: Both feel force of size eE, in opposite directions; a = eE/m, and m_p/mₑ ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷/9.1 × 10⁻³¹ ≈ 1840 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two charges 40 cm apart in air are moved into an oil of dielectric constant 4. At what separation, in metres, will the force between them be the same as it was in air?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2} = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{Kr'^2} \Rightarrow r' = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{K}} = \dfrac{0.40}{\sqrt{4}} = 0.20$ m.
